item.title: Tupelo police seek help identifying shoplifting suspects - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
TUPELO – Crime Stoppers of Northeast Mississippi and the Tupelo Police Department are asking for the public’s help identifying people involved in a reported shoplifting incident.

Authorities said the incident happened April 28, 2026, in Tupelo.

Police are asking anyone who recognizes the suspects in the attached photos or has information about the incident to contact Crime Stoppers of Northeast Mississippi.

Tips can be submitted by calling 800-773-TIPS, or by using the P3 Tip App.

Crime Stoppers said it may pay up to $2,000 for a tip that leads to an arrest.

Tipsters can remain anonymous.

item.title: Silver Alert issued for missing Jackson man - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Mississippi Bureau of Investigation has issued a Silver Alert for a missing Jackson man.

Authorities said 63-year-old Charles Dana Kirkland Jr. was last seen Sunday, May 3, at about 5:40 p.m. in the 100 block of Hayes Drive in Hinds County.

Investigators said Kirkland was walking east when he was last seen. He was wearing a gray hoodie, gray sweatpants and white shoes.

Kirkland is described as 6 feet tall and weighing about 200 pounds. He has blonde hair and blue eyes.

Family members told authorities Kirkland suffers from a medical condition that may impair his judgment.

Anyone who sees Kirkland is asked to call the Jackson Police Department at 601-960-1234 or 911.

item.title: Mississippi proposes updates to park fees, fishing limits and hunting regulations - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks is proposing a series of changes to park fees, fishing and boating permits, and hunting regulations, with public comment now open for the next 30 days.

The proposed updates were presented during the April meeting of the Mississippi Commission on Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks and would affect state parks, fisheries and wildlife management rules statewide.

Among the proposed park changes are adjustments to age ranges for annual permits and boat launch fees, adding ages 16 and older to daily fishing fees and lowering the senior age classification from 65 to 62. The department also plans to rename “fishing permits” as “boating permits” to better align with current regulations.

Fisheries proposals include updated crappie limits at Lake Mary Crawford, Simpson County Lake and Horseshoe Lake, as well as revised largemouth bass regulations at several public fishing lakes. Officials also proposed changes to bream limits at Simpson County Lake and a no-harvest rule for walleye at Elvis Presley Lake.

Commercial fishing regulations could also change, including reducing mesh size requirements for hoop nets and prohibiting the possession or transport of live catfish measuring 34 inches or larger.

Wildlife officials are proposing new restrictions for turkey hunting, including reducing the nonresident seasonal bag limit from three birds to two. Nonresident hunters would be limited to one bird before April 1, and all hunters would be restricted to one bird during Wildlife Management Area draw hunts.

According to the department, the proposed changes reflect input from anglers and hunters and aim to align Mississippi’s rules with those in neighboring states while maintaining sustainable wildlife populations.

The proposals are available for public review and comment for 30 days on the department’s website.

The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks said its mission is to conserve and enhance the state’s natural resources while providing quality outdoor recreation opportunities.

item.title: Mississippi appeals court revives wrongful death lawsuit over 2021 death of Damien Cameron - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — A Mississippi appeals court has revived a wrongful death lawsuit against two Rankin County sheriff’s deputies and the county itself, ruling Monday that disputed facts about how deputies restrained Damien Cameron before his July 2021 death must be decided by a jury.

The Mississippi Court of Appeals voted 7-3 to reverse the summary judgment in favor of Deputies Hunter Elward and Luke Stickman, finding factual disputes about whether their use of force was excessive and whether they were entitled to qualified immunity. The court also reversed summary judgment for Rankin County on state law claims. The decision was issued May 5.

Cameron, who was known as “Toot,” died after deputies arrested him at his home on Foote Drive in Braxton following a vandalism complaint at a neighbor’s house. A toxicology report later found methamphetamine in his system. The state medical examiner listed the cause and manner of death as “undetermined.”

Cameron’s mother, Monica Lee, sued Rankin County, Elward and Stickman, alleging the deputies used excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment and state law under the Mississippi Tort Claims Act.

At the center of the dispute is what happened after Stickman arrived to help Elward handcuff Cameron. Lee and her parents told Mississippi Bureau of Investigation agents that Stickman knelt on Cameron’s neck as he lay prone on the floor, and that Cameron repeatedly said he could not breathe. Stickman said in his report that he knelt beside Cameron with minimal pressure on his back.

The plaintiffs’ expert, Dr. Shandelle Norford, concluded to a reasonable degree of medical probability that Cameron died of cardiopulmonary arrest caused by neck and back compression from both officers during restraint, which she termed “restraint associated asphyxia” with methamphetamine as a contributing factor.

Writing for the majority, Chief Judge Virginia Carlton Barnes said those conflicting accounts created questions of fact that a circuit court cannot resolve at summary judgment.

“Taking into account the consistent testimony by Lee and her parents that Damien repeatedly told the deputies that ‘he couldn’t breathe’ after both deputies subdued him by using their body weight to kneel on his back and neck, we find there was a genuine issue of fact whether these actions constituted a prohibited ‘choke hold’ under the County’s policies and procedures and were excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment,” Barnes wrote.

The Rankin County Sheriff’s Department’s own use-of-force policy expressly prohibits choke holds, defined to include applying pressure to a person’s neck. Sheriff Bryan Bailey acknowledged in a deposition that if a deputy applied force to Cameron’s neck with a knee, it would have violated that policy.

The majority also pointed to Elward’s subsequent criminal conviction for falsifying incident reports as a factor bearing on his credibility, and cited a Fifth Circuit ruling that it is a question of fact for a jury to determine whether a person who appeared to be resisting was “merely trying to get into a position where he could breathe.”

The court additionally found a factual dispute over a third use of a Taser, this time in drive-stun mode on Cameron’s thigh after he had already been handcuffed and placed partially in a patrol car, noting Cameron had been tased twice before and had been asserting that he could not breathe.

In a partial dissent joined by Judge John Emfinger and in part by Presiding Judge Jack Wilson, Judge Lassitter St. Pé argued the circuit court reached the right result and should have been affirmed. She wrote that the undisputed evidence showed Cameron actively resisted throughout the encounter and that the deputies ceased using force once he was restrained.

“By reversing that decision, the majority substitutes speculation for evidence and weakens the protections afforded by both qualified immunity and the summary judgment framework,” Lassitter St. Pé wrote.

The appeals court unanimously upheld the circuit court’s denial of Lee’s motion to file a second amended complaint, which sought to add Monell claims and supervisory liability allegations against Rankin County. The court found the motion was filed three weeks past the scheduling order’s deadline and would have caused undue prejudice to the defendants.

The case now returns to Rankin County Circuit Court. The excessive force claim against the individual deputies will be decided by a jury; the state law claim against Rankin County under the Mississippi Tort Claims Act will be decided by the trial judge.

item.title: Jackson Public Schools apologizes for unintentional Facebook post - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Jackson Public Schools apologized Tuesday after content was unintentionally posted on the district’s official Facebook page.

District officials said the post was removed immediately after the error was identified.

JPS said appropriate steps are being taken to make sure content intended for the district’s official platform is managed separately from personal platforms.

The district said it cares about broader societal issues and their impact on scholars and communities, but does not take a public stance on political matters.

Jackson Public Schools said it remains a nonpartisan organization.

The district apologized to scholars, families, staff and the broader community for what it called a misrepresentation and for any concern it may have caused.

item.title: FEMA warns Mississippi disaster survivors of assistance scam - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – The Federal Emergency Management Agency is warning Mississippi disaster survivors about scammers asking for money to complete disaster assistance applications.

FEMA said scammers are targeting survivors by requesting a $150 payment to complete an application for assistance.

The agency said it does not charge anyone to apply for disaster assistance. FEMA is urging residents not to send money or share personal information with anyone claiming payment is required.

Officials said FEMA staff always carry official photo identification, and residents should confirm they are speaking with an agency employee before providing any information.

FEMA said it works with the Department of Homeland Security and the U.S. Department of Justice to protect disaster assistance and investigate fraud.

Anyone who suspects fraud can call the Disaster Fraud Hotline at 866-720-5721 or visit fema.gov/disaster-fraud.

item.title: Dr. Jelani C. Zarif inspires JSU graduates to see degrees as pathways to leadership - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
By Anthony Howard and Jatavian Walker Jackson State University

JACKSON — Jackson State University honored its Spring 2026 graduate class during commencement exercises at the Lee E. Williams Athletics and Assembly Center, celebrating students whose academic journeys reflected perseverance, global scholarship and personal triumph.

JSU’s 14th president, Denise Jones Gregory, Ph.D., presided over her first commencement ceremony since being named in April. She said the Spring 2026 graduating class reflects the university’s mission of academic excellence, leadership development and student success, noting that the graduates continue to demonstrate resilience and readiness to serve communities locally and globally.

“Jackson State University is proud to celebrate the Class of 2026 and all they have accomplished to reach this moment,” said Gregory. “Commencement is a special time on our campus. It marks the work our students have put in and the people who supported them along the way. We are grateful to everyone who helped make this moment possible and look forward to recognizing our graduates as they step into this next chapter.”

The ceremony featured keynote remarks from Dr. Jelani C. Zarif at the Jackson State University Spring 2026 Graduate Commencement Ceremony, who encouraged graduates to embrace resilience, purpose and long-term growth.

“It’s not necessarily a sprint; it’s a journey—and the journey is worth it,” said Zarif, an award-winning researcher who holds the Robert E. Meyerhoff endowed professorship at the Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center. He urged graduates to reframe challenges as preparation for leadership and impact.

“There will be moments when the path feels uncertain,” he said, emphasizing that success is built through sustained effort and perseverance. “But those moments are not meant to break you—they are meant to build you.”

Zarif also challenged graduates to view their degrees as a call to service. “Your degree is not just a personal achievement— it is a responsibility to serve, to lead and to uplift others.”

Among the graduates was Tameka J. Battle from Jackson, Mississippi, who earned an Education Specialist degree in K–12 Administration and Supervision while overcoming a breast cancer diagnosis.

Battle said she continued her academic work throughout treatment with support from JSU faculty and staff. “This degree was very hard for me,” she said. “While within the program here at Jackson State, I was diagnosed with breast cancer.”

She added that perseverance and support carried her through the program. “My professors and my department chair… worked with me as far as getting my courses done,” she said. “But God gave me the strength and the power to accomplish this goal.”

Battle shared that she was diagnosed as cancer-free in February 2026.

The ceremony also recognized Edna Carolyn Frazier McCallum, a member of JSU’s “Golden Class,” who returned to campus decades after first earning her degrees in music and education.

McCallum reflected on her longstanding connection to the university. “I loved every minute of Jackson State,” she said. “I just loved the music industry.”

She noted the significance of returning alongside family generations connected to JSU. “I’m so proud that she followed in my footsteps,” she said, referencing her granddaughter, a 2023 JSU graduate.

Graduate Shadrack Barffour Awuah from Ghana earned a master’s degree in Public Health after completing undergraduate medical studies in Ukraine. He said JSU’s research focus drew him to the university.

“I love Public Health,” Awuah said. “Reading through how they are very active in research was the main reason why it led me to come here [Jackson State].”

Southern New Jersey native and doctoral graduate Armando Rijo earned a Ph.D. in Urban Higher Education. He credited JSU’s cohort model and academic community for supporting his success.

“It was a great experience,” Rijo said. “They really held me down and kept me moving throughout the entire program.”

item.title: Central Mississippi Turtle Rescue seeks transport for injured turtle - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
FOREST – Central Mississippi Turtle Rescue is asking for help transporting an injured turtle from Forest to the Jackson area.

According to the rescue, the turtle was found in the jaws of a dog and needs to be brought to the organization for care.

The rescue said the finder does not have transportation and cannot meet volunteers at another location.

Volunteers are needed to transport the turtle from Forest to the Jackson area. The rescue said it also has an offer from someone who can bring the turtle in if another volunteer can transport it from Forest to Morton.

Central Mississippi Turtle Rescue said it can reimburse gas at 14 cents per mile for someone making a special trip to transport the turtle.

Anyone who can help is asked to contact Central Mississippi Turtle Rescue.

item.title: Carroll County man arrested on drug charge after search warrant - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
CARROLL COUNTY — A 22-year-old man was arrested after deputies executed a search warrant at a residence in the McCarley area, authorities said.

Deputies with the Carroll County Sheriff’s Office carried out the warrant Friday, May 1, and reported finding a large amount of marijuana, U.S. currency and digital scales during the investigation.

Brandon Joseph Watt was taken into custody and charged with possession of a controlled substance with intent to sell, officials said.

Watt was booked into the Carroll County Regional Correctional Facility, where bond was set at $25,000. He was released on bond Monday.

Sheriff Clint Walker credited deputies for their work on the case and said efforts to combat illegal drugs will continue.

“Illegal drugs promote gun violence, as well as property crimes, and impaired driving,” Walker said. “We will continue to work tirelessly to stop the flow of illegal drugs in our county.”

The association said the heron can be returned to its flower box under the mural with no questions asked.

Anonymous tips can be sent to [email protected] .

item.title: Blood drive being held today to support Ridgeland Police Cpl. Ryan Stacy - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
RIDGELAND- Mississippi Blood Services is hosting a blood drive Tuesday to support Cpl. Ryan Stacy of the Ridgeland Police Department.

Cpl. Ryan Stacy was hurt in a crash on the Natchez Trace Parkway during severe weather, after his vehicle struck a fallen tree. The crash happened April 26th.

The blood drive will be held today (Wednesday) from 2 p.m. to 7 p.m. at the Ridgeland Police Department, located at 115 West School Street in Ridgeland.

Mississippi Blood Services said donors who cannot attend the Ridgeland event can still support Stacy by donating at the Flowood Donor Center and using code ES24. That code will allow the donation to be credited toward him.

Mississippi Blood Services encouraged eligible donors to give blood to help save lives.

Ridgeland PD asks public to help injured officer

item.title: Why do we celebrate Cinco de Mayo? - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Mary Apel
item.description:
Cinco de Mayo, or May 5th, falls on Tuesday this year. Although it is often mistaken as Mexico’s Independence Day, it actually commemorates the Mexican army’s victory over the French army at the Battle of Puebla on May 5, 1862.

The origins of what we call Cinco de Mayo can be traced back to the mid-19th century when Mexico was struggling with economic woes and political instability. At the time, Mexico had incurred significant debt to European countries, including France, Britain, and Spain.

In 1861, Mexican President Benito Juarez declared a moratorium on the repayment of foreign debts, which led to a military invasion by French forces. The French army, led by Napoleon III, aimed to establish a French-supported monarchy in Mexico, which would provide a valuable ally in the Americas.

However, the Mexican army, led by General Ignacio Zaragoza, fiercely resisted the French forces and defeated them at the Battle of Puebla on May 5, 1862. This victory, although not decisive in the war, became a symbol of Mexican resistance against foreign intervention and marked a significant historical moment for Mexico.

Cinco de Mayo remained a relatively minor holiday in Mexico until the late 20th century, at which point it gained widespread popularity in the United States. After the Mexican Civil War ended in 1915, many Mexican people came to the United States and settled in the southern states. When they came to America, they brought with them their customs, traditions, and holidays—including Cinco de Mayo.

The holiday became a way for Mexican-Americans to celebrate their culture and heritage, and to share it with their neighbors in the US. Additionally, the holiday’s popularity has been fueled by commercial interests, with many businesses using it as an opportunity to promote Mexican food, drinks, and other products.

Want to celebrate at home? Then combine lime juice, Triple Sec, white (blanco) tequila, and ice in a blender for a frozen drink or a shaker for one on-the-rocks. Serve with some chips and salsa, and enjoy!

Authorities said the incident happened around 8 a.m. when a witness reported that his goddaughter had been kidnapped from a home.

Authorities are also asking anyone who sold or transferred a white Ford Escape to Timothy Davis Jr. in the Sumrall area to contact investigators immediately.

Police said Davis has a criminal history that includes burglary, felony mischief, auto theft, trespassing, grand larceny and other charges.

Anyone with information is asked to call the Jackson Police Department at 601-960-1800.

item.title: Mississippi State opens new livestock evaluation laboratory to support students, industry - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
STARKVILLE — Mississippi State University has opened a new Livestock Evaluation Laboratory designed to enhance student training and support the state’s livestock industry.

The ribbon-cutting ceremony for the facility was held Monday by the university’s College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the Mississippi Agricultural and Forestry Experiment Station.

University officials said the new laboratory provides a dedicated, modern space for livestock judging and evaluation, a program that has been part of Mississippi State since the 1920s. The facility includes a workroom, lounge, office and conference room, along with a multipurpose open-air arena for live practice and competitions.

MSU President Mark E. Keenum said the lab will benefit students as they prepare for careers in agriculture.

“The new Livestock Evaluation Lab will benefit current and future generations of students and help ensure their success as they earn their degrees and begin their careers,” Keenum said.

U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who attended the event, was among those recognized for supporting the project.

The MSU Livestock Judging Team, housed in the Department of Animal and Dairy Sciences, trains multiple times each week and travels frequently for competitions, with students spending an average of 36 weekends each year competing.

Scott Willard, dean of the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and director of the experiment station, said the facility will strengthen the program by providing a dedicated space for practice and events.

“Livestock evaluation builds confidence and strengthens our students’ problem-solving skills as they present their analyses and defend their reasoning to judges,” Willard said.

Funding for the project included private donations through the Rodney Moore and Family Livestock Judging Facility Support Fund, established by alumni and supporters of the program.

University leaders said the facility is expected to enhance hands-on learning opportunities for students while contributing to the continued growth of Mississippi’s agricultural sector.

item.description:
JACKSON – Mississippi’s hand-grabbing season is now open, giving anglers across the state a chance to take part in one of Mississippi’s more unusual fishing traditions, according to the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks.

The season runs from May 1 through July 15, the department said.

Hand-grabbing, sometimes called noodling, involves reaching into underwater holes to catch catfish by hand. Wildlife officials said Mississippi is one of the few states with a dedicated season for the practice.

The department said some of the largest blue and flathead catfish caught in Mississippi each year are taken during hand-grabbing season.

MDWFP encouraged interested anglers to review regulations and season information before heading out.

item.title: MDWFP opens applications for 'Fire on the Forty' prescribed burn program - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks is now accepting applications for its “Fire on the Forty” program, which helps private landowners use prescribed fire to improve wildlife habitat and land management.

Officials said the 2026 application period opened May 1 and will run through June 19. Approved projects will be funded through April 30, 2027.

The program promotes the use of controlled, or prescribed, burns on private lands to support native plant growth, reduce invasive vegetation and lower the risk of more destructive wildfires. Prescribed fire is widely considered a key tool for managing forests and wildlife habitats across the South, but many landowners avoid it due to cost and liability concerns.

Through the initiative, eligible landowners in selected counties may receive reimbursement for up to 75% of the cost of conducting prescribed burns, up to a maximum per-acre rate.

Applications are competitively ranked based on factors such as potential habitat benefits, with funding decisions made by Mississippi Partners for Fish and Wildlife.

The program also includes an educational component, offering workshops that combine classroom instruction with hands-on field experience. Topics include fire planning, safety, ignition techniques and legal considerations. Workshops are held across the state, often in partnership with agencies such as the Mississippi Forestry Commission and Mississippi State University Extension Service.

Since its launch in 2015, the program has supported prescribed burns on more than 100,000 acres of private land and provided training to more than 1,200 landowners. It has also been recognized nationally, receiving a 2026 Land Stewardship Award from the National Wild Turkey Federation.

Officials said the program’s broader goal is to create connected habitat areas that benefit wildlife such as bobwhite quail and rabbits, while encouraging more landowners to adopt prescribed burning practices.

More information, including application details and workshop schedules, is available through the Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks.

item.title: Kitten rescued from storm drain in Jackson after dayslong effort - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – A kitten is safe after being rescued from a storm drain in Jackson following a dayslong effort involving the Animal Rescue Fund of Mississippi and Jackson Water, according to the rescue.

The Animal Rescue Fund of Mississippi said it was contacted after people had spent three days trying unsuccessfully to free the kitten from the drain.

When rescuers arrived, they determined they needed additional help and called Jackson Water to assist with opening a nearby manhole.

The rescue said the kitten was trapped between the storm drain and the manhole in several inches of water and appeared frightened, cold, wet and dehydrated.

Workers and rescuers tried multiple methods to coax the kitten toward them, including using a plumbing snake to gently encourage it to move, according to the group.

Eventually, rescuers played recorded sounds of a mother cat calling her kitten. The rescue said that drew the kitten close enough for one of the rescuers to grab it safely.

The kitten, later named Raphael after the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, was taken back to the shelter for care.

The rescue said Raphael is now stable and beginning his recovery.

item.title: Better Sleep Month highlights health risks, benefits of quality rest - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Health experts are urging Mississippians to take sleep more seriously as Better Sleep Month is observed in May, emphasizing that consistent, quality rest is essential to physical health, mental well-being and daily performance.

Better Sleep Month, recognized each year, aims to raise awareness about the importance of sleep and the consequences of going without it. A survey by the Better Sleep Council found two out of three respondents reported disrupted sleep due to stress, and about one-third of Americans experience poor sleep at least once a week.

The effects can extend well beyond fatigue. The National Sleep Foundation reports that 45% of Americans say poor or insufficient sleep affected their daily activities at least once in the past week.

Sleep deprivation is also a public safety concern. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, fatigue contributes to an estimated 100,000 motor vehicle crashes and about 1,550 deaths each year in the United States.

Health officials say adults should aim for at least seven hours of sleep per night. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention notes that getting enough sleep can reduce the risk of chronic conditions such as heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes and stroke, while also improving mood, memory and overall functioning.

Quality of sleep is just as important as duration. The CDC reports that interrupted or non-restorative sleep can leave people feeling tired even after spending enough time in bed.

During sleep, the body carries out critical processes including tissue repair, immune system support and memory consolidation. Mental health is also closely tied to sleep, with research showing that inadequate rest can increase stress, anxiety and difficulty regulating emotions.

To improve sleep, experts including the Mayo Clinic recommend maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, creating a cool, dark and quiet sleep environment and limiting screen use before bedtime. Avoiding caffeine late in the day and large meals close to bedtime can also help.

For those who continue to struggle with sleep, health officials advise consulting a medical provider to evaluate for possible sleep disorders such as insomnia or sleep apnea.

Better Sleep Month was established in 1978 by the Better Sleep Council, the consumer education arm of the International Sleep Products Association, to promote awareness of the connection between sleep and overall health. Officials say the message remains clear: getting enough quality sleep is a key part of staying healthy.

item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — Some of y’all really are sports fans to the death. Like literally, to the death.

A new national survey examining the emotional ties between sports fans and their favorite teams found that Mississippi fans would most want their ashes scattered at two of the state’s most iconic college football stadiums.

Not surprisingly, it’s Davis Wade Stadium and Vaught-Hemingway Stadium.

item.title: Ridgeland Students Launch ‘WORTH A LISTEN’ Mental Health Initiative - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
RIDGELAND — Students with the Ridgeland Mayor’s Youth Council are launching a new mental health awareness initiative aimed at reducing stigma, increasing access to resources and encouraging conversations among young people across the metro area.

The initiative, called “WORTH A LISTEN,” is a collaboration between the youth council, Killebrew Psychological Services and Essential Touchstones.

Organizers said the student-led effort will initially roll out in six metro-area schools attended by members of the Ridgeland Mayor’s Youth Council, with plans to eventually expand statewide. The program will include student-led awareness campaigns, mental health resource distribution, school and community outreach efforts, and partnerships with local and state mental health organizations.

Ridgeland Mayor Gene McGee said the initiative reflects growing concerns about the mental health challenges facing students.

“Young people today are facing pressures and challenges unlike any generation before them,” McGee said. “‘WORTH A LISTEN’ sends a powerful message that their voices matter, their struggles are seen, and help is always available.”

According to organizers, the idea for the initiative emerged after students applying to the Mayor’s Youth Council were asked to identify the biggest issues affecting their peers. Officials said 95% of applicants cited mental health concerns, including anxiety, depression, bullying and social media addiction.

Lisa Walters, the mayor’s chief of staff and coordinator of the youth council, said the responses made it clear the issue could not be ignored. Mental health professionals with Killebrew Psychological Services and Essential Touchstones later joined the effort to help shape the program and provide clinical guidance.

Dr. Alyssa Killebrew said the initiative is especially meaningful because it is being driven by students themselves.

“What makes this initiative so powerful is that it is coming directly from students who recognize the need among their own peers,” Killebrew said.

National research cited by organizers shows youth mental health concerns continue to rise. Studies from organizations including the National Alliance on Mental Illness and the American Psychological Association indicate that nearly 40% of high school students report persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness, while roughly two in five young people experience a diagnosable mental health condition each year.

Student leaders involved in the initiative said they hope the program encourages peers to seek help and support one another.

“So many students feel like they have to handle everything on their own,” said Ashwin Talwar, a member of the youth council. “This initiative is about making sure everyone knows there is someone who will listen and that it’s okay to ask for help.”

City leaders said they hope “WORTH A LISTEN” becomes a long-term movement focused on improving mental health awareness and support systems for students throughout Mississippi.

item.title: Pearl River County search warrant turns up suspected marijuana, THC vapes and cash - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
PICAYUNE – Two people were arrested after a narcotics search warrant was executed at a residence in Picayune, according to the Pearl River County Sheriff’s Department.

The sheriff’s department said its Narcotics Division, with help from the Patrol Division, served the warrant April 29 at a home on Cabin Drive.

During the search, investigators seized what authorities described as a large quantity of suspected marijuana, THC vape products, digital scales, packaging materials and U.S. currency believed to be tied to illegal drug distribution.

The sheriff’s department identified the two occupants as Catherine Zirkle, 24, and Dylan Revolta, 24, both of the Cabin Drive address in Picayune.

Both were taken to the Pearl River County Criminal Justice Facility and charged with trafficking a controlled substance and possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance, according to the sheriff’s department.

Sheriff David Allison thanked deputies and investigators for their work in combating illegal drug activity in Pearl River County.

Anyone with information about narcotics activity is asked to contact the Pearl River County Sheriff’s Department at 601-403-2582.

item.title: Mississippi opens statewide applications for private land alligator tags for 2026 season - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Mississippi landowners across the state can now apply for private land alligator tags for the 2026 season, according to the state’s private lands and permits information.

Officials said the private lands alligator tag program is available statewide beginning in 2026.

Applications for private lands alligator permits will be accepted from May 1 through July 1, and all applications must be submitted online, according to the state.

There is no fee to apply.

Officials said anyone may submit an application for a property in open counties as long as the landowner signs the application. Only one application may be submitted for each property.

The 2026 alligator season opens on the last Friday in August, which falls on Aug. 28 this year.

According to the state, the private lands season will run from noon Aug. 28 until 6 a.m. Sept. 21.

item.title: Mississippi Attorney General finds use of force justified in four line of duty shootings - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Attorney General’s Office announced Monday it has completed reviews of four line of duty shootings across the state and determined the use of force was justified in each case.

According to the Attorney General’s Office, the reviews were conducted following investigations by the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, as required under Mississippi law.

One of the incidents reviewed occurred July 9, 2022, in Jackson and involved an officer with the Jackson Police Department near the former Canton Apartments on Southwest Street. This was during a period of time when Jackson Police Department was not releasing all information to the media or the public and we’re working to confirm what happened.

Another case stemmed from a Feb. 21, 2024, pursuit in Lake Cormorant involving deputies with the DeSoto County Sheriff’s Office. Investigators said deputies executed a PIT maneuver after a vehicle pursuit near U.S. 61 south of Mississippi 3. Authorities said the suspect, identified as 35-year-old Jamarcus Brown, fired at a K-9 after deputies released the dog. Deputies returned fire, killing Brown. The K-9, Luca, suffered serious injuries and later died shortly before retirement.

The Attorney General’s Office also reviewed an Oct. 15, 2024, shooting in Jackson involving a Jackson police officer. Police said the incident began on Interstate 220 after a collision involving a stolen Volvo. Authorities alleged 47-year-old Anthony Johnson fired shots at an 18-wheeler driver before later pointing a weapon at narcotics detectives, who then shot him in the lower extremities. Johnson was charged with two counts of aggravated assault on a law enforcement officer and possession of a stolen vehicle.

The fourth incident occurred Dec. 31, 2024, in Ridgeland and involved a detective with the Ridgeland Police Department. Investigators said detectives located a stolen vehicle at Renaissance at Colony Park near Barnes & Noble. Authorities said a 15-year-old suspect struck a detective with the vehicle as officers approached. The detective fired his weapon, striking the suspect, who then fled before crashing near Watkins Drive and Interstate 220. The teen was later arrested and charged with multiple offenses, including aggravated assault on a police officer and receiving stolen property.

The Attorney General’s Office said all four reviews concluded the officers’ actions were legally justified under Mississippi law.

item.title: MISSING IN MISSISSIPPI: Elester Womack, Covington County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
COLLINS — Nearly four years after he disappeared, the whereabouts of Elester Womack remain unknown, and the lack of information about it leaves investigators searching for answers.

Womack, also known to family and friends as “Farrell,” was last seen on or around June 3, 2022, in Covington County, according to the Covington County Sheriff’s Department.

Very few details have been released publicly about the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

At the time he vanished, Womack was 61 years old. He is a Black male with black hair and brown eyes, standing 5 feet 7 inches tall and weighing about 178 pounds.

Authorities and family members have continued to ask the public for information in hopes of generating new leads in the case.

Older adults represent a smaller share of missing persons cases nationwide, but advocates say those disappearances can present unique challenges. FBI missing person data shows hundreds of thousands of people are reported missing in the United States each year, including tens of thousands of adults. Cases involving seniors can involve anything from medical conditions to confusion to foul play or unexplained circumstances like Womack.

Metro Crime Stoppers joined the search effort, offering anonymous tip options and possible cash rewards for information leading to progress in the investigation.

Anyone with information about Womack’s disappearance is urged to contact the Covington County Sheriff’s Department at 601-765-8281 or Metro Crime Stoppers at 601-582-STOP. Tips may also be submitted online through P3Tips.com .

item.title: JSU twins honor late father, earn master’s in speech-language pathology - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Special to Darkhorse Press
item.description:
By William H. Kelly III Jackson State University

JACKSON — Twin sisters Ebonee and Ebonea’ Harrison, 28, earned their master’s degrees in speech-language pathology and audiology from Jackson State University, accomplishing yet another major milestone together.

The St. James Parish, Louisiana, natives graduated on Friday, May 1, celebrating sisterhood and stepping into a career they chose in honor of their late father.

Prior to their birth, their father endured a tragic collision with a train that left him in a week-long coma, paralyzed on one side of his body, and unable to speak due to a traumatic brain injury. Sadly, as they approached their 16th birthday, the girls and their father were caught in a devastating car accident with a drunk driver that ultimately took his life.

Growing up, the twins’ mom would play home videos and share stories about their dad’s recovery and how physical therapy and a speech pathologist were instrumental in restoring his mobility and voice back to “normal.”

“For him to be able to communicate and still be able to express himself, and take care of us, was a big thing. It was an eye-opener for us, and we wanted to come into this field based on that,” they shared. “We wanted to come into this career and change lives as well.”

Speech-language pathologists utilize tools such as Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) devices, Picture Exchange Communication System® (PECS®), and non-verbal gestures to assist people with communicating.

“Everyone’s voice deserves to be heard no matter what, and everyone deserves a chance to communicate,” Ebonea’ shared.

While navigating the graduate program at JSU the siblings’ passion for speech-language pathology grew deeper through hands-on clinical training at facilities like Brookdale Senior Living in Clinton, Methodist Rehabilitation and Smart Therapy, LLC, Pediatric Rehabiliation Clinic.

The twins learned to service children and adult clients who ranged from being non-verbal, blind, hearing impaired, and autistic, or suffered from dementia, strokes, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and more.

Both Ebonee and Ebonea’ believe that interacting directly with patients reminded them of the role they hope to serve in communities throughout Mississippi and Louisiana.

“Being in our clinical placements showed us how hard it is for some people to communicate, and the big role we play in their lives to help them communicate,” said Ebonee. “Communication is essential for life, and everyone should be able to communicate in some aspect.”

Ebonee and Ebonea’ look forward to what’s next. They currently have over three job offers at the same skilled nursing facility, pediatric clinic, and elementary school.

“I love this field, and being here really made me love it even more. It didn’t sway me away,” said Ebonea’. “I learned a ton at Jackson State University that I don’t think I would have learned anywhere else.”

item.title: Hurricane Awareness week offers Mississippi a familiar reminder: Be prepared - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
JACKSON — The Mississippi Gulf Coast has faced the order to evacuate at least seven times since Hurricane Katrina reshaped the coastline in 2005. For residents of the southern counties, the drill is practically institutional: pack up, load the car, head north on I-55, I-59, or MS-49 and hope for the best.

But hope is not a preparedness plan.

Governor Tate Reeves has declared May 3-9 as Hurricane Preparedness Week, and both the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and the Mississippi Insurance Department are using the occasion to push residents toward concrete action before the Atlantic hurricane season officially begins June 1.

“Over the last several years, our state has confronted many natural disasters including hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, and ice storms,” Reeves said. “It is critical to have a plan before severe weather strikes. It can make a difference in keeping you and your family safe. I hope Hurricane Preparedness Week can help raise awareness about the upcoming hurricane season and encourage Mississippians to take the necessary steps to prepare.”

Last year’s Atlantic season produced 13 named storms, five of which became hurricanes and four of which intensified into major hurricanes, just above the historical average of three major hurricanes per season, according to the National Weather Service.

That proximity to average can be deceiving. The Gulf Coast has learned repeatedly that it does not take a record-breaking season to produce catastrophic results. Gustav and Ike hit in back-to-back weeks in September 2008, forcing two rounds of coastal mobilization within the same season.

Hurricane Isaac in 2012, a slow-moving Category 1 that might have seemed manageable on paper, triggered mandatory evacuations in all three coastal counties, dropped 17 inches of rain on Kiln, and ultimately housed more than 2,100 evacuees in shelters statewide.

Hurricane Zeta in 2020 caused an estimated $1.25 billion in damage to the coast, knocked out power to roughly half a million customers, and put more than 3,000 people in shelters. Hurricane Ida prompted mandatory evacuations across low-lying areas of Hancock County just a year later.

The pattern stretches back two decades and beyond, to the storm that still defines the conversation: Hurricane Katrina. Waveland, nearly wiped off the map by Katrina’s storm surge in 2005, did not get its police department back into a permanent building until 2016 , eleven years after the storm. The lesson the coast learned at enormous cost is the same one state officials are repeating this week: the time to prepare is before the season starts, not after the forecast cone appears on the evening news.

“I encourage all Mississippians to use Hurricane Preparedness Week to prepare now, by assembling an emergency supply kit, developing a family emergency plan, and determining evacuation routes,” said MEMA Executive Director Stephen McCraney. “By taking precautions now, we can safeguard our communities from any potential tropical storms. Let’s work together to ensure the safety and resilience of Mississippi during this hurricane season.”

MEMA will highlight a specific preparedness topic each day of the week on its social media platforms, moving from “Know Your Risk” on Sunday through “Take Action Today” on Saturday. A full disaster supply checklist is available at msema.org , along with MEMA’s Hurricane Preparedness Guide in English, Spanish and Vietnamese.

On the insurance side, Commissioner Mike Chaney is flagging a detail that catches many homeowners off guard.

“Don’t forget to review your insurance coverage and make sure you are familiar with your policies,” Chaney said. “Flood insurance takes 30 days to go into effect after it’s bought. Some insurance policies have a special deductible for losses caused by named storms. The insurer applies this deductible only when a named storm causes damage. This deductible is separate and different from the normal deductible in a homeowners policy.”

That 30-day window matters more than most people realize. When a storm is already in the Gulf, it is too late to buy flood coverage. MEMA echoes that advice, encouraging homeowners to complete an insurance review now and to purchase flood insurance if their home sits in a special flood hazard zone.

Both agencies recommend households take two additional steps this week.

item.description:
STARKVILLE – A coach and an umpire were both charged after officers responded to a fight at Cornerstone Park, according to the Starkville Police Department.

item.title: Beloved Malayan tiger Bunga undergoing treatment at Hattiesburg Zoo - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
HATTIESBURG – The Hattiesburg Zoo says Bunga, its Malayan tiger, is undergoing medical treatment for several health concerns, including high blood pressure and significant disc disease.

According to the zoo, Bunga had two nosebleed episodes about two weeks ago and was later diagnosed with hypertension. Hattiesburg Zoo veterinarian Dr. Julia MacGregor started him on medication to manage the condition.

The zoo said Bunga initially showed some improvement, but staff noticed changes in his behavior late last week, including increased lethargy and signs of discomfort.

Zoo officials said Bunga was taken Wednesday to Animal Medical Center in Hattiesburg, where he underwent a CT scan to look for possible underlying causes of his symptoms.

The scan showed significant disc disease, especially in his neck, which the zoo said is likely causing discomfort and some mobility changes. Bunga’s bloodwork was largely normal, according to the zoo.

“Bunga’s case is complex, and our team is working diligently to manage multiple conditions at once,” MacGregor said in a statement. “Our immediate priority is to keep him comfortable while stabilizing his blood pressure.”

The zoo said its veterinary team has adjusted Bunga’s medications by increasing treatment for his blood pressure and adding pain management for chronic and nerve-related discomfort.

Zoo officials said Bunga has shown sensitivity to certain medications in the past, so staff are carefully balancing treatment to make sure it is both safe and effective.

Bunga is also continuing treatment for inflammatory bowel disease, a condition the zoo said he was diagnosed with last year.

The zoo said animal care staff are monitoring him closely and that all decisions are being made with his quality of life as the top priority.

“Our focus is always on Bunga’s wellbeing,” zoo officials said. “We are committed to providing the highest level of care and making thoughtful, compassionate decisions every step of the way.”

MacGregor also praised the zoo’s veterinary and animal care teams for training Bunga to voluntarily participate in parts of his care, including blood draws and blood pressure checks. The zoo said that training allows for more frequent monitoring without the need for full immobilization.

Bunga has been a longtime favorite among visitors and serves as an ambassador for Malayan tigers, which are critically endangered, according to the zoo.

The Hattiesburg Zoo said it will continue to monitor Bunga and share updates when appropriate.

item.title: Attorney General Lynn Fitch joins 41 attorneys general urging feds to leave sports betting oversight to states - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Morgan Howard
item.description:
JACKSON – Mississippi Attorney General Lynn Fitch has joined a bipartisan coalition of 41 attorneys general urging federal regulators to reaffirm that states, not the federal government, should oversee sports-related event contracts tied to betting.

According to Fitch’s office, the coalition filed a formal comment with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission arguing that so-called prediction markets have effectively become unregulated sportsbooks.

“Mississippi, like many states, has carefully balanced competing interests to allow responsible sports betting here,” Fitch said in a statement. “The CFTC should not upend that balance, usurp state authorities without a clear Congressional directive, and leave states with the responsibility for cleaning up the impacts of sports betting without the ability to regulate it on the front end.”

The coalition said prediction market platforms allow users to wager on outcomes such as game winners, point spreads and player statistics while bypassing state gambling regulations and consumer protections.

In the comment letter, the attorneys general argued that there is no meaningful difference for consumers between traditional sports bets and sports-related event contracts offered on designated contract markets.

The coalition contends that those contracts do not serve the traditional purposes of derivatives markets, such as hedging or price discovery, and instead function as entertainment-based gambling, which they say falls under state authority.

The attorneys general also warned that sports gambling can pose risks to public health and financial security and said states are better equipped than the CFTC to regulate or prohibit such activity.

The letter was filed in response to a CFTC request for public comment on proposed rules for prediction markets. The coalition urged the agency to confirm through rulemaking that it does not have jurisdiction over sports-related contracts.

Fitch joined attorneys general from 40 other states and the District of Columbia in signing the letter.

item.title: Ruth man killed in two-vehicle crash in Lincoln County - Darkhorse Press
item.author: Therese Apel
item.description:
LINCOLN COUNTY — A 40-year-old man from Ruth was killed Friday morning in a two-vehicle crash in Lincoln County, according to the Mississippi Highway Patrol.

Troopers responded to the crash around 8 a.m. on May 1 on Highway 84.

Authorities said Jeffery Grimes was driving a 2015 Volkswagen Passat north on East Lincoln Road when his vehicle collided with a 2016 Ford F-150 traveling east on Highway 84. The pickup was driven by 30-year-old Alexis Bass of Natchez.

Grimes suffered fatal injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene, officials said.

No additional injuries were immediately reported.

The crash remains under investigation by the Mississippi Highway Patrol.
